SCORING_RULES: Consistent = earns the level. One good rep does not qualify.
Any single item on the failure list = level not met.
Speed or trail complexity can trigger any failure mode.
Assess under real trail conditions whenever possible.
Assess at start of every season — skills regress in off-season.

SCALE.consistency: Falls apart on anything beyond flat
Falls apart with distraction or challenge
Falls apart only at extreme consequence

body_position.name: Body Position
body_position.description: Foundation for Braking and Cornering. Three skills build in order: (1) ready position for the terrain, (2) Body Bike Separation (BBS) side-to-side and front-to-back, (3) pumping and pressure control.
body_position.calibration_note: Most riders reach Level 2 without much coaching. Level 3 is a realistic goal for a full season of coaching. Level 4 is rare — few riders reach it. Level 5 is elite, and beyond what NICA trails require.
notes: At Levels 1–2, weight shifts are accidents — the rider doesn't mean to move. At Levels 4–5, weight shifts are on purpose — the rider is loading the bike to handle a feature.

levels.2: Controlled spots like a parking lot or grass field. Sometimes on easy trail.
levels.3: On trail most of the time. Drops back to old habits when the ride gets hard.
levels.4: Always on trail, on any terrain. Rarely has to think about it.
levels.5: Always in the right position, even without thinking about it. Applies pressure control on every feature. Beyond what NICA trails require.

levels.1: Knees pinch saddle, or rider sits instead of standing in ready position. Locked arms and legs. Looks down at the front wheel. The 3 Key Essentials are missing or inconsistent.
levels.2: Stands, but stays stiff. Does not switch between tall and low ready as the trail changes. Loses ready position when surprised or challenged. The 3 Key Essentials fail too.
levels.3: Picks tall or low ready correctly most of the time. The 3 Key Essentials hold, even with some distraction. Reverts to a stiff, front-wheel stare only when badly over-challenged.
levels.4: Always picks the right ready position for the terrain. The 3 Key Essentials are automatic. Almost never reverts.
levels.5: Low ready is automatic in any condition. Uses ready position to ride better, not just to stay upright.

levels.1: No forward or back motion. Rider stays locked in one spot. Weight shifts are stiff and out of control.
levels.2: Weight shifts forward or back by accident — habit, confusion, or fear. BBS F/B is missing or barely there.
levels.3: BBS F/B shows up most of the time. Falls apart on technical climbs or steep descents.
levels.4: BBS F/B is always there. Shifts on purpose for features — for example, forward on a roll-down or step-up.
levels.5: F/B pressure control is automatic. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201).

levels.1: No side-to-side motion. Rider looks stiff on the bike.
levels.2: BBS S/S is minimal. Any motion disappears with a small challenge.
levels.3: BBS S/S shows up most of the time, including on trail. Shrinks or disappears on off-camber ground or in hard corners.
levels.4: BBS S/S is always there on trail, on any tread or camber. Rarely disappears, even with a surprise.
levels.5: BBS S/S holds in any condition. Rider actively uses it to ride better.

levels.1: Not aware that tire pressure changes with terrain.
levels.2: Aware that weight shifts change tire pressure, but the shifts are still accidental.
levels.3: Starts loading features on purpose. Still inconsistent.
levels.4: Loads features on purpose, every time. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201).
levels.5: Full pressure control on any terrain. Foundation for wheelies and manuals (OTB-301). Beyond what NICA trails require.

1.detail: Knees pinch saddle, or rider sits instead of standing in ready position. Rigid on the bike, so no BBS is possible. Looks at the front wheel. The 3 Key Essentials are missing: no bend in elbows and knees, elbows not wide, weight not in the feet.

adds: May be able to ride standing, out of the saddle
progression.terrain: Smooth, predictable ground — packed dirt, grass, or a paved path
how_to: Teach OTB-101 ready position. Practice in easy conditions.
Cue: heavy feet, light hands. Deep bend in elbows and knees.
Game: follow-the-leader, with the leader showing correct position.
Start on grass or pavement so terrain isn't competing for attention.

2.consistency: Falls apart with distraction or challenge
2.detail: Stands, but stays rigid. Weight shifts forward or back by accident — from habit, confusion, or fear. Does not switch between tall and low ready as the trail changes. BBS S/S and F/B are missing or minimal. The 3 Key Essentials fail with distraction or challenge.

adds: Stands in ready position consistently
3 Key Essentials hold in calm conditions
Shows BBS with coaching
resolves: No longer seated or pinching the saddle with the knees
Eyes no longer locked on the front wheel
progression.terrain: Smooth, predictable ground — packed dirt, gentle grade, no real obstacles
how_to: Static ready-position holds to learn heavy feet
Ride ready position on slightly harder terrain — small bumps and rollers — to build trust in the bike
Cue: heavy feet, light hands. Deep bend in elbows and knees.
Game: red light, green light — ridden entirely in ready position
Start on grass or pavement so terrain isn't competing for attention

3.consistency: Good when easy, falls apart when over-challenged
failure_modes: Pressure control only starting to appear
3.detail: Picks tall or low ready correctly most of the time. The 3 Key Essentials hold reliably. BBS S/S and F/B show up most of the time. Pressure control starts to appear on purpose, but is still inconsistent. Reverts to a stiff, front-wheel stare only when badly over-challenged.

adds: BBS side-to-side and forward/back appear on trail
Picks tall or low ready to match the terrain
3 Key Essentials hold reliably, not just when calm
resolves: Less rigid — body and bike are no longer locked together
Weight no longer shifts forward or back by accident
Ready position no longer lost to ordinary distraction
progression.terrain: Rolling singletrack with roots, rocks, and small features; moderate grade
how_to: BBS S/S drill: figure-8s at walking pace, letting the bike lean under a quiet upper body
Rollers and water bars to introduce BBS forward/back on purpose
Cue: let the bike move under you. Keep heavy feet, light hands.
Add speed and distraction slowly. Back off the moment form slips.

4.consistency: Falls apart only at extreme consequence
failure_modes: Barely has to think about it
4.detail: Always picks the right ready position for terrain and features. The 3 Key Essentials are automatic. BBS S/S and F/B are always present. Loads features on purpose — for example, a lunge on a roll-down or step-up. Pressure control is consistent. Foundation for front wheel lifts (OTB-201). Largely automatic — takes little conscious thought.

adds: Loads features on purpose, every time
Switches between tall and low ready on any terrain
Barely has to think about the movement anymore
Sees weight shifts coming and adjusts early
resolves: BBS no longer falls apart when over-challenged
No longer reverts to a stiff posture or a front-wheel stare
progression.terrain: Varied terrain with roots and rocks, drops and rollers; often loose, often steep
how_to: Lunge drills on roll-downs and step-ups to build deliberate loading
Pump track or rolling-terrain laps for continuous pressure-control practice
Practice pressure control while cornering and braking
Cue: push the bike into the back side of the feature, not just over the top
Raise the stakes slowly — form must hold on the trail, not just in the drill

failure_modes: Full pressure control on any terrain, on purpose
5.detail: Ready position is automatic in any condition. Pumping and pressure control are automatic across every feature and terrain. Foundation for wheelies and manuals (OTB-301). Fully automatic, with tactical use. Beyond what NICA trails require.

adds: Pumping and pressure control are automatic on any terrain
Chooses body position for the feature ahead, on purpose
Foundation for wheelies and manuals (OTB-301)
resolves: Holds even when the stakes are high
No longer stays in ready position when neutral is better
progression.terrain: Sustained steep and loose terrain, large features and drops — beyond what NICA courses require
how_to: Advanced pressure-control work: wheelies, manuals
Repeat hard features, changing line and speed
Beyond what NICA trails require — coach only if the athlete wants to pursue it

braking.name: Braking
braking.description: Builds on ready position. Three skills build in order: (1) both brakes, with modulation, (2) bracing leg and hips back, (3) timing brakes for corners and the trail.
braking.calibration_note: Most riders operate at Level 1–2. Level 3 is a meaningful goal for a season of coaching. Level 4 takes real experience and trail time.
notes: Emergency braking test: coach puts an unexpected obstacle in the rider's path. This shows whether braking form holds up under surprise — the real test of whether braking has become automatic. Level 4 requires passing this test consistently on trail.

levels.2: Controlled setting, with warning before the stop. Reverts to old habits when the stop is a surprise.
levels.3: On trail most of the time. Fails at extreme speed or the hardest surprise stops.
levels.4: Always solid on any trail terrain — planned and emergency stops. Barely has to think about it.
levels.5: Solid in any condition. Manages brakes on purpose, tactically. Beyond what NICA trails require.

levels.1: Rear brake only, or mostly rear brake. Two or three fingers on the levers — no modulation possible. Grabs the brakes and skids. Afraid to brake hard, so can't slow down well. Brakes in corners by default.
levels.2: Even front and rear brake in calm conditions. A surprise stop yanks the rear brake only and skids. Brakes in corners as a panic response to speed or consequence.
levels.3: Good modulation — rarely skids. Powerful braking with a short stopping distance. Front and rear balance is consistent.
levels.4: Never skids. Uses both brakes every time. Modulation is fully consistent. Always brakes before the corner.
levels.5: Precise modulation, timing, and front/rear pressure in any condition. Carries speed late, then brakes hard to a precise entry speed. Feels traction loss in real time and adjusts.

levels.1: Upper body shifts forward under hard braking. No weight management. Uncomfortable braking hard.
levels.2: Upper body shifts forward on surprise stops. Some rearward shift on stops the rider sees coming.
levels.3: Hips back and down is starting to show up — still learning. Present sometimes on normal stops. Not yet reliable under pressure or surprise.
levels.4: Hips back and down is automatic on every stop, including surprises.
levels.5: Full pressure control — releases the front brake first, then trails the rear to settle the suspension. Holds the rear brake through steep corners to manage speed. Times braking to the best-traction zones.

levels.2: Present on stops the rider sees coming. Lost on surprise stops.
levels.3: Consistent, except on the hardest surprise stops.
levels.4: Always automatic — planned stops and emergencies. Passes the emergency braking test consistently on trail.
levels.5: Holds in any condition, including trail braking through corners.

1.consistency: Falls apart on anything beyond flat
1.detail: Rear brake only, or mostly rear brake. Two or three fingers on the levers — no modulation possible. Grabs the brakes and skids. Afraid to brake hard, so can't slow down well. Brakes in corners by default.

2.detail: Even front and rear braking in calm conditions. A surprise stop yanks the rear brake only, and skids. Upper body shifts forward, making the skid worse. Bracing leg shows up on stops the rider sees coming, but is lost on surprise stops. Brakes in corners as a panic response to speed or consequence.

adds: Uses both brakes evenly in calm conditions
One finger on each lever
Bracing leg shows up on stops the rider sees coming
resolves: No longer rear-brake-only
No longer grabs the levers into a skid when prepared
Less afraid to brake hard — can actually slow the bike down
progression.terrain: Gentle grade with good traction; stops the rider can see coming
how_to: Braking box: stop inside a marked zone with both brakes. Make the box shorter over time.
Cue: squeeze, don't grab — one finger per lever
Add the bracing leg: drop the heel, stiffen the front leg on every stop
Repeat until form holds on every stop the rider expects

failure_modes: Bracing leg lost at extreme surprise
Hips back and down: learning, not yet reliable
3.detail: Good modulation — rarely skids. Powerful braking with a short stopping distance. Bracing leg is consistent, except on the hardest surprise stops. Hips back and down is starting to show up — still learning, present sometimes on normal stops, not yet reliable under pressure or surprise. Holds body position well enough to move into cornering.

adds: Modulation good enough that skids are rare
Powerful braking with a short stopping distance
Hips back and down starts to show up
Bracing leg holds except on the hardest surprise stops
resolves: No longer yanks the rear brake when surprised
Upper body no longer pitches forward under hard braking
No longer brakes in corners as a panic response
progression.terrain: Moderate descents with mixed traction; stops that come up quickly
how_to: Surprise-stop reps: coach calls the stop late so braking must survive the surprise
Cue: hips back and down — get behind the saddle as the brakes come on
Brake-before-the-corner drill: finish all braking before turn-in
Vary the surface so modulation is trained, not just force

4.consistency: Falls apart only at extreme consequence
4.detail: Never skids. Uses both brakes every time. Braking is always solid on any terrain — planned and emergency stops. Hips back and down is automatic. Always braces the leg, including emergencies. Brakes before the corner every time. Braking form holds up on surprise stops — passes the emergency braking test on trail.

adds: Hips back and down automatic on every stop
Bracing leg always present, including emergencies
Braking always finishes before the corner
Form holds up when a surprise obstacle appears
resolves: Never skids
Braking form no longer falls apart under surprise or consequence
progression.terrain: Steep, loose, and rutted descents; sudden unplanned stops
how_to: Emergency braking test on trail: an unexpected obstacle in the rider's path, repeated until form holds
Steep-descent braking with a full hips-back position
Cue: brake early and hard, then release smoothly into the corner
Assess across varied tread — loose, wet, and hardpack

5.detail: All the basics of braking are always correct. Precise modulation, timing, and front/rear pressure on purpose, in any condition. Carries speed late, then brakes hard to a precise entry speed — releases the front brake first, then trails the rear to settle the suspension. Holds the rear brake through steep corners to manage speed. Feels traction loss on slippery ground and adjusts in real time.

adds: Precise modulation and timing, tuned to conditions
Carries speed late, then brakes hard to an exact entry speed
Releases the front brake first and trails the rear to settle the suspension
Feels traction loss in real time and adjusts
resolves: Braking essentially never falls apart, in any condition
progression.terrain: Sustained steep ground with poor traction and no run-out — beyond what NICA courses require
how_to: Trail-braking practice through long, steep corners
Traction experiments on purposely loose ground
Beyond what NICA trails require

cornering.name: Cornering
cornering.description: The longest skill sequence. Skills build in order: Level 2 adds BBS side-to-side lean and holding ready position. Level 3 adds Low-Look-Lean plus hip rotation and counterbalance. Level 4 makes the full sequence consistent. Level 5 adds pumping and pressure control through the apex.
cornering.calibration_note: Most riders reach Level 2. Level 3 needs consistent BBS and the start of hip rotation — a realistic goal for a full season for riders who train regularly.
notes: Panic is the consistency axis: weight back, braking in the corner, squeezing the bike, and steering instead of leaning are common panic responses. A higher level means a higher panic threshold.

Level 2 check: correct BBS S/S lean looks like this — inside elbow straightens, outside elbow bends sharply, seat shifts toward the inside thigh. Go back to the BBS S/S drill if body and bike are still locked together.

levels.1: Flat, predictable ground. Slow speed only.
levels.2: Controlled setting. Sometimes on easy trail with clear corners.
levels.3: Easy trail most of the time. Reverts to old habits at higher speed or consequence.
levels.4: Always consistent on blue and black terrain. Barely has to think about it. Panic is rare.
levels.5: Any condition. Fully automatic. Panic is essentially absent. Beyond what NICA trails require.

levels.1: Pedals uneven, or inside pedal down. Seated — no ready position.
levels.2: Outside or inside pedal down. Seated, or tall ready, entering the corner.
levels.3: Pedals level on entry most of the time. Low ready shows up but fades mid-corner.
levels.4: Pedals level every time. Low ready holds through the whole corner.
levels.5: Level pedals and low ready are automatic in any condition.

levels.1: No bike lean, or leans to the outside. Steers through every corner.
levels.2: Body and bike lean together, locked — knees squeezed, no BBS S/S. Steers instead of leaning. Eyes on the threat instead of the exit.
levels.3: BBS S/S lean is consistent — correct direction, knees wide, elbows hinge, seat shifts toward the inside thigh. Lean stays within the OTB-101 range.
levels.4: BBS S/S lean is always consistent. Lean angle matches speed and corner. Eyes stay on the exit every time.
levels.5: BBS S/S holds in any condition.

levels.3: Shows up in ideal conditions — visibly more lean than BBS alone. Not present under pressure.
levels.4: Always consistent on blue and black terrain. Lean angle reflects hip rotation the whole way through.
levels.5: Holds in any condition, including high speed and mixed tread.

levels.1: Weight too far forward or back — no awareness of it.
levels.2: Weight too far forward or back — from habit, confusion, or fear. Happens in both directions at this level.
levels.3: Weight generally centered. Loses front/back balance under pressure. No pressure control yet.
levels.4: Weight stays stable through the corner. Pressure control shows up in ideal conditions — consistent banked corners.
levels.5: Pumps the apex — loads the bike on purpose through the corner peak and mid-corner features. Depends on momentum. Beyond what NICA trails require.

levels.1: Panics at a low threshold — steers, brakes in the corner, weight back.
levels.2: Panics at moderate speed — brakes in the corner, weight back, squeezes the bike and steers.
levels.3: Same panic pattern, but a higher threshold. Usually clean on normal trail riding.
levels.4: Panic is rare. Not present in normal trail riding. Recovers quickly.
levels.5: Panic is essentially absent. Correct movement holds even at extreme speed and consequence.

1.consistency: Falls apart on anything beyond flat
1.detail: Setup: pedals uneven, or inside pedal down. Seated — no ready position. Lean: no bike lean, or leans to the outside. Steers through every corner. Eyes: on the front tire or the threat — this makes speed feel faster and triggers panic.

2.consistency: Falls apart at faster or unpredictable corners
failure_modes: Body and bike locked in the same lean
2.detail: Setup: outside or inside pedal down. Seated, or tall ready, entering the corner. Lean: body and bike lean together, locked — knees squeezed, no BBS S/S. May lean to the outside. Steers instead of leaning, especially under speed. Eyes: on the front tire or the threat, instead of through the exit. Panic: brakes in the corner, weight back, squeezes the bike and steers to compensate.

adds: Level pedals more often than not on entry
Stands in ready position through the corner
The bike starts to lean instead of only being steered
resolves: No longer seated through every corner
No longer steers through every corner
Pedals no longer uneven or inside-pedal-down
progression.terrain: Wide, flat corners with good traction and a clear view ahead
how_to: Set the corner up first: level pedals and low ready before turn-in
BBS S/S drill: figure-8s, letting the bike lean under a still upper body
Cue: knees wide — squeezing the bike locks out the lean
Look-ahead game: coach holds up fingers at the corner exit so the eyes leave the front tire

3.consistency: Falls apart at higher speed or consequence
failure_modes: BBS lean falls apart under pressure
Hip rotation only in ideal conditions
3.detail: Setup: pedals level on entry most of the time. Low ready shows up but fades mid-corner. Lean: BBS S/S lean is consistent — correct direction, knees wide, elbows hinge, seat shifts toward the inside thigh. Lean stays within the OTB-101 range. Hip: hip rotation and counterbalance show up in ideal conditions only. Eyes: through the exit most of the time. Reverts to old habits under pressure.

adds: BBS S/S lean is consistent — inside elbow straightens, seat shifts toward the inside thigh
Hip rotation and counterbalance show up in ideal conditions
Eyes through the exit most of the time
resolves: Body and bike no longer locked in the same lean
Knees no longer squeeze the bike
Eyes no longer locked on the threat
Panic happens less often — the threshold has risen
Weight no longer too far forward or back through the corner
progression.terrain: Tighter corners carrying speed; some off-camber and loose tread
how_to: Low-Look-Lean as one sequence, called out loud through each corner
Hip rotation drill (OTB-201): rotate the inside hip toward the exit, counterbalance with the outside arm
Cue: seat toward the inside thigh — the bike leans more than the body
Session one corner repeatedly, adding speed only while the sequence holds

4.consistency: Falls apart only at extreme consequence
failure_modes: Hip rotation falls apart at extreme consequence
Pressure control only on consistent banked corners
Barely has to think about it
4.detail: Setup: pedals level every time. Low ready holds through the whole corner, every time. Lean: BBS S/S is consistent. Hip: hip rotation and counterbalance are always consistent on blue and black terrain. Eyes: on the exit every time. Rarely reverts to old habits. Weight: stable through the corner. Pressure control shows up in ideal conditions — consistent banked corners.

adds: Full sequence is consistent on blue and black terrain
Lean angle matches speed and corner shape
Low ready holds through the whole corner
Pressure control starts to show up on consistent banked corners
Weight stays stable through the whole corner
resolves: Lean and hip rotation no longer fall apart under speed or consequence
Ready position no longer fades mid-corner
Panic is rare in normal trail riding

how_to: Corner sessions at higher entry speed on varied camber
Berm pumping: load the bike through the apex of banked corners
Cue: pressure through the apex, eyes already on the next corner
Add off-camber and rutted corners to test the sequence

5.detail: The full sequence holds in any condition — rocky, off-camber, loose, rutted, with drop exits. Pumps the apex: loads the bike on purpose through the corner peak for maximum traction. Applies this to mid-corner features like roots, rolls, and drops. Depends on momentum — can't be held still.

adds: Pumps the apex — loads the bike on purpose through the corner peak for maximum traction
Sequence holds on rocky, off-camber, loose, rutted corners, and drop exits
Panic is essentially absent
resolves: Cornering essentially never falls apart, at any speed or consequence
progression.terrain: Rocky, rutted corners with drops at the exit — beyond what NICA courses require
how_to: Mid-corner feature work: roots, rolls, and drops inside the arc
Momentum-dependent pumping drills — the load can't be held still
Beyond what NICA trails require

TRAIL_GUIDE.intro: Trail selection is a safety decision. It needs a current skill assessment. Not a memory from last season. Not a guess based on fitness or speed. Not just one observation. Skills fade in the off-season. Every rider needs a current assessment before the season's trail decisions are made.
TRAIL_GUIDE.minimums_note: These are the minimum skill levels needed to ride a trail class at trail speed. They are a floor, not a ceiling. A higher-rated rider can ride lower-rated trails. A lower-rated rider may ride short sections of a harder trail — by slowing down or walking the technical features.
TRAIL_GUIDE.trail_ratings_note: A trail's difficulty rating comes from its hardest feature, not its average character. The coach's job: find which specific feature earns the trail its rating. Check whether riders have the minimum skill for that feature. Set the minimum based on the feature, not just the trail's overall rating.
assessment_rules: Assess during skills instruction, skills sessions on trail, and normal riding.
The rider must show the skill in varied conditions on that trail type. For example: through corners, over water bars, at speed, on different tread.
Keep correcting the rider until the skill is solid. It should show up reliably, on more than one ride.
Any item on the failure list means the level is not met. Speed or trail difficulty can trigger any failure mode.
TRAIL_GUIDE.real_example: A blue trail with features was picked for early-season riders. The coach remembered them as 'really good.' Skills were not assessed at the start of the season. Skill levels observed on trail: Body Position 1–2, Cornering 1. Minimum needed for this trail: Body Position 3, Cornering 2. One rider crashed. A stiff body position on a small feature was the direct cause. The rider was not hurt. But the crash was predictable — the gap showed up because no assessment was done.
TRAIL_GUIDE.score_notation: Scores are written as Body Position – Braking – Cornering, like 2-3-2.
score_examples: New rider at 1-1-1. Goal: reach 2-2-1 before the first trail ride.
Ride group baseline: bring every athlete to 2-2-2 by the start of the season.
Varsity target: 3-3-3, to safely ride blue trails.
TRAIL_GUIDE.reassessment: Every two weeks, on the same reference section. Pick a section that tests cornering, BBS, braking, and body position all at once.

COACH_NOTES.fitts_posner: The 1–5 scale matches the three stages of motor learning from Fitts and Posner. NICA coach training covers this. Levels 1–2 are the cognitive stage — movements are conscious, inconsistent, and fail under distraction. Level 3 is the associative stage — movements are getting reliable, but still fall apart under pressure. Level 4 is mostly automatic. The rider barely has to think about the basic movement, which frees them to focus on terrain and tactics. Level 5 is fully automatic, with tactical use on top. Reaching Level 4 is a real achievement. Reaching Level 5 is elite.
COACH_NOTES.calibration: Most riders operate at Level 1–2. That's not a failure — it reflects where developing athletes are, given limited trail time. Moving from Level 1 to Level 2 is a real achievement, worth recognizing. Level 3 is a realistic goal for riders who train consistently for a full season. Level 4 is genuinely rare — fewer than a dozen riders across 12 seasons of IICL coaching have shown it consistently. Level 5 is elite skill, beyond what NICA trails require.
common_errors: Confusing fitness with skill. A strong climber who steers through corners is still Level 1 in cornering.
Scoring the best performance instead of the consistent one. 'Most of the time' earns Level 3, not Level 4.
Assessing on flat ground only — most skills fall apart on steeper or rougher ground.
Treating Level 4–5 as the same as 'fast.' Speed is not part of the rubric.
Using last season's assessment. Skills fade in the off-season. Assess at the start of every season.
interdependencies: Braking Level 3 needs Body Position Level 2 or higher.
Cornering Level 3 needs Body Position Level 2 and Braking Level 2.
At Levels 1–2, weight shifts are accidents. At Levels 4–5, on-purpose F/B pressure control is correct execution.
key_essentials: A finger on each brake lever at all times
